extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric, classical oratory, and prose style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging classical rhetorical prose (oratorical style), describing when to use smoothness, force, abruptness, rhythm, and which stylistic choices are faults. Aimed at writers/orators seeking effective composition techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness of composition (such as is employed particularly by the followers of Isocrates, who avoid the concurrence of vowels) is not altogether suited to forcible language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth, euphonious phrasing suits elegant or eulogistic discourse but can weaken forcible passages. Example: recasting a sentence to avoid vowel-clashes may 'rob them of a good part of their force.' Use smoothness when the aim is harmony and elegance; avoid it when you need blunt force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vowel-clash/hiatus for force
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases greater force will result from an actual clashing [of vowels], as ... the very clang of clashing vowels may be held to make a sentence more forcible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate collision of vowels (hiatus) can heighten vigor and emphasis in heated passages. Example: the original phrasing about the Phocian war is stronger because of its clang. Do not mechanically smooth such collisions when wanting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and unpremeditated diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Words which are actually unpremeditated, and are as it were a spontaneous growth, will give an impression of vigour, especially when we are manifesting our anger or our sense of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural, apparently spontaneous phrasing conveys passion and authenticity. Conversely, anxious attention to niceties of smoothness signals 'elegant trifling' rather than genuine anger. Favor candid, immediate diction in passionate or accusatory passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abruptness as a rhetorical figure
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'figure' of abruptness has a forcible effect. The same may now be said of abrupt composition on a larger scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abrupt sentences or breaks can produce forceful effect; used at scale, abrupt composition can sustain intensity. Use abruptness to stop, start, or shock the reader/listener, but deploy it intentionally to avoid seeming disjointed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken rhythm for invective
rubrics_metrics.description: By destroying the rhythm, [Hipponax] made the measure suitable for energetic invective, since correct and melodious rhythm would be fitter for eulogy than for satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disrupting regular rhythm (shattered verse / broken cadence) is appropriate for invective and scorn; regular, melodious rhythm better serves praise. Match rhythmic choice to the rhetorical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of bombast
rubrics_metrics.description: He shuns the bombast which is apt to beset not only rhetorical historians like Cleitarchus but writers on Style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overblown, grandiose language (bombast) undermines credibility and invites ridicule. Be wary of inflated metaphors and swelling cadences, especially in genres not calling for them (e.g., history or technical exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpleasant style (avoid disgusting detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Side by side with the forcible style there is found ... a corresponding faulty style, called 'the unpleasant.' It occurs in the subject matter when a speaker mentions publicly things which are disgusting and defile the lips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid graphic, sordid, or vulgar details that contaminate the speech and repulse the audience (example: needlessly public descriptions of filth or sexual scandal). If the goal is force, rely on warranted invective rather than gross particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disjointed, unlinked members
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition has an unpleasant sound, if it seems disjointed ... when the members are in no way linked to one another, but resemble fragmentary pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain logical and syntactic linkage between clauses and sentence-members. Fragmentary, poorly connected sequences produce an 'unpleasant' effect and reduce clarity and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessively long continuous periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, continuous periods which run the speaker out of breath cause not only satiety but actual aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit lengthy, breathless sentences. Break up overly long periods into manageable units to maintain audience attention and avoid fatigue or irritation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction and imagery to subject (avoid frigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often objects which are themselves pleasant enough lose their attractiveness owing to the words applied to them ... The result is that the passage is both unpleasant and frigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metaphors, epithets, and descriptive language suit the object. Misapplied, overwrought, or incongruent imagery (e.g., describing a wasp with figures fit for a boar) produces frigidity and alienates the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force can be pleasant or coarse
rubrics_metrics.description: Force may be pleasant; it may also be coarse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for force that is rhetorically attractive rather than merely coarse or vulgar. Evaluate whether vigorous phrasing elevates the argument or merely shocks in a way that diminishes effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate rhythm and euphony
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct and melodious rhythm would be fitter for eulogy than for satire ... Smoothness of composition ... is not altogether suited to forcible language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rhythmic and euphonic devices according to genre: harmonious cadence for praise and solemn subjects; rough or broken sound for satire, invective, or energetic denunciation. Avoid one-size-fits-all sound patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive nicety of style when expressing passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxious attention to niceties of smoothness and harmony does not betoken anger so much as elegant trifling and a desire to exhibit one’s powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sincere passion is required, prioritize forceful, natural expression over polished ornament. Over-refinement in heated passages can undermine perceived authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate use (and avoidance) of stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, rhythm, compounds, and sound-effects can contribute to elevation, force, or vividness, but they must be used with discrimination; peculiar figures and dithyrambic compounds should be avoided in the plain style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rhetorical devices (figures of speech, compounds, sound-patterns) according to the chosen stylistic type (elevated, elegant, forcible, plain). Excess, misuse, or genre-mismatch of such devices causes frigidity, obscurity, or aridity.
